about: Sourced life stories for the Jerusalem church and its first witnesses: James and Jude the Lord's brothers, Stephen, Philip the evangelist, Barnabas and John Mark. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/church-jerusalem.md.

james-mat-13-55.short: Named first of Jesus' brothers by the people of his own country; Paul saw "James the Lord's brother" at Jerusalem, and names James among the "pillars".

paragraphs.text: When Jesus taught in the synagogue of his own country, the people asked, "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon?" Matthew gives the same four brothers, James first, and both Gospels speak of sisters who are not named. Scripture does not say how James and the other brothers were related to Mary and Joseph; the answers that have been given are set out on his page.

The Gospels also speak of Jesus' brethren as a group, without naming them. They went down to Capernaum with him and his mother, and once they came with his mother and stood outside, calling for him. When the feast of tabernacles was near they urged him to go into Judaea and show himself, "For neither did his brethren believe in him." Scripture does not say whether James was with them each time.

Paul writes that the risen Lord "was seen of James", but he does not say which James. After Jesus was taken up, his brethren were in prayer with the apostles and with Mary the mother of Jesus. Paul also writes that "the brethren of the Lord" had the right to "lead about a sister, a wife", as the other apostles did; he does not name them.

Paul writes that "after three years" he went up to Jerusalem to see Peter and stayed with him fifteen days: "other of the apostles saw I none, save James the Lord's brother." Later in the same letter he says that James, Cephas and John, "who seemed to be pillars", gave him and Barnabas "the right hands of fellowship", agreeing that Paul and Barnabas should go to the heathen and they to the circumcision; they asked only that Paul and Barnabas remember the poor. At Antioch, Peter ate with the Gentiles until "certain came from James", and then he withdrew.

After Herod had killed James the brother of John, Acts still names a James. Peter, freed from prison, said, "Go shew these things unto James, and to the brethren". At the council in Jerusalem, after Peter, Barnabas and Paul had spoken, this James quoted the prophets and said, "my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God". He asked only that they be told to keep from the pollutions of idols, fornication, things strangled and blood, and the apostles and elders, with the whole church, sent a letter. Acts never calls this James the Lord's brother; his page takes him to be the same man by setting Acts beside Galatians.

The last time Acts names him, Paul came to Jerusalem and "went in with us unto James; and all the elders were present". Paul told what God had done among the Gentiles; they glorified the Lord and advised Paul to purify himself with four men who had a vow. The letter of James opens "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" without saying which James. Scripture does not say when James came to believe, whether he married, or how he died.

jude-mat-13-55.short: One of the four brothers of Jesus named by the people of his own country, "Juda" in Mark and "Judas" in Matthew; Scripture records nothing he said or did.

paragraphs.text: Jude is one of the four brothers the people of Jesus' own country named when he taught in their synagogue: "James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon". Mark spells the name Juda and Matthew Judas, and both Gospels speak of sisters who are not named. Scripture does not say how the brothers were related to Mary and Joseph; the answers that have been given are set out on his page.

Beyond those two lists, Scripture speaks of Jesus' brethren only as a group. They went down to Capernaum with him and his mother; when the feast of tabernacles was near, "neither did his brethren believe in him"; after Jesus was taken up they were in prayer with the apostles and Mary; and Paul writes that "the brethren of the Lord" had the right to "lead about a sister, a wife". None of these passages names Jude.

Scripture says very little about him. The letter of Jude opens "Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James"; it does not say which James, and Scripture does not say whether its writer is this Jude. Luke's list of the Twelve has a "Judas the brother of James", and Scripture does not say whether he is this Jude either. It records nothing Jude said or did, and nothing of his death.

stephen-act-6-5.short: One of the seven chosen at Jerusalem, "full of faith and of the Holy Ghost"; stoned after his speech to the council, he prayed for those who stoned him.

paragraphs.text: Stephen first appears in the church at Jerusalem, when the Grecians complained that their widows were neglected in the daily ministration. The Twelve asked the disciples to choose seven men "of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom", and Stephen was named first, "a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost". The seven were set before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them. Scripture names no family, home town or trade for him.

Stephen, "full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people." Some "of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia" disputed with him, but "they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake". They then got men to say that he had spoken blasphemous words against Moses and against God, stirred up the people, the elders and the scribes, and brought him to the council. There false witnesses said that he spoke against "this holy place, and the law", and all who sat in the council saw "his face as it had been the face of an angel".

When the high priest asked, "Are these things so?", Stephen answered with the story of Israel: God's call to Abraham, Joseph sold into Egypt, and Moses, "whom they refused", whom God sent as a ruler and a deliverer. He spoke of the tabernacle in the wilderness and the house Solomon built, and said, "the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands". He ended by calling his hearers "stiffnecked": "as your fathers did, so do ye", and he said they had been the betrayers and murderers of "the Just One".

His hearers were cut to the heart and gnashed on him with their teeth. Stephen, "full of the Holy Ghost", looked up into heaven and said, "I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God." They cast him out of the city and stoned him, and the witnesses laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen called, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit", knelt down, and cried, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge"; and "he fell asleep".

Saul "was consenting unto his death", and devout men carried Stephen to his burial "and made great lamentation over him". A great persecution followed and all but the apostles were scattered; those scattered "upon the persecution that arose about Stephen" travelled as far as Phenice, Cyprus and Antioch, preaching the word. In Acts 22 Paul recalls saying to the Lord, "when the blood of thy martyr Stephen was shed, I also was standing by, and consenting unto his death".

philip-act-6-5.short: One of the seven chosen at Jerusalem, later called "Philip the evangelist"; he preached in Samaria, baptized an Ethiopian official, and had a house at Caesarea.

paragraphs.text: Philip was named second of the seven men chosen at Jerusalem when the Grecians' widows were neglected in the daily ministration: men "of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom", whom the apostles prayed over and on whom they laid their hands. The Twelve had asked for them so that they could give themselves "to prayer, and to the ministry of the word". He is a different man from Philip the apostle, one of the Twelve; Acts later calls him "Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven".

After Stephen's death a great persecution scattered the church at Jerusalem, all but the apostles, and those who were scattered went everywhere preaching. Then "Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them". Unclean spirits came out of many, the lame and those taken with palsies were healed, and "there was great joy in that city". Men and women believed and were baptized, among them Simon, who had used sorcery there and who then "continued with Philip"; when the apostles at Jerusalem heard of it, they sent Peter and John.

Then an angel of the Lord sent Philip south to the way from Jerusalem to Gaza, "which is desert". The Spirit told him to go near the chariot of an Ethiopian, a eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who was reading the prophet Esaias; Philip asked him, "Understandest thou what thou readest?" Beginning at the same scripture, Philip "preached unto him Jesus", and when they came to water he baptized him. "The Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip", and the eunuch "went on his way rejoicing".

Philip "was found at Azotus", and he preached in all the cities until he came to Caesarea. Later, when Paul's company came to Caesarea, they stayed in "the house of Philip the evangelist". "The same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy." While they were there the prophet Agabus bound his own hands and feet with Paul's girdle and said that the Jews at Jerusalem would bind its owner.

Acts does not call the Philip of chapter 8 "one of the seven"; he is taken to be the evangelist because the apostles had stayed at Jerusalem and Acts leaves him at Caesarea, where the evangelist lived. Scripture does not say where Philip came from, how he came to believe, or why he is called "the evangelist". It does not name his daughters or tell how he died.

barnabas-act-4-36.short: A Levite of Cyprus whom the apostles surnamed Barnabas; he vouched for Saul, taught with him at Antioch, and travelled with him until they parted over Mark.

paragraphs.text: His name was Joses, and the apostles surnamed him Barnabas, "which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation". He was a Levite from Cyprus; he had land, sold it, and laid the money at the apostles' feet. When Saul came to Jerusalem and the disciples were all afraid of him, Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the way and had preached boldly at Damascus.

When the church at Jerusalem heard that a great number at Antioch had believed, it sent Barnabas there. He "was glad, and exhorted them all" to cleave unto the Lord, and Acts calls him "a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith". He went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him to Antioch, where for a whole year they taught many people, and "the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch". When a famine was foretold, the disciples sent relief to the elders in Judaea "by the hands of Barnabas and Saul".

Barnabas and Saul came back from Jerusalem bringing "John, whose surname was Mark". Barnabas heads the list of the "prophets and teachers" in the church at Antioch, and there the Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them." They fasted, prayed, laid hands on them and sent them away, and the two sailed to Cyprus, with John as their minister. In Colossians Paul calls a Marcus "sister's son to Barnabas".

On Cyprus the deputy Sergius Paulus called for Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God. From there they came to Perga, where John left them, and went on to Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. At Lystra the people called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius, and Acts calls them "the apostles, Barnabas and Paul" as they rent their clothes and scarcely kept the people from sacrificing to them. They came back through the cities, ordained elders, and told the church at Antioch how God "had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles".

When men from Judaea taught the brethren that they could not be saved unless they were circumcised, Paul and Barnabas disputed with them and went up to Jerusalem about the question. There the multitude heard Barnabas and Paul tell of the wonders God had done among the Gentiles, and the church's letter called them "our beloved Barnabas and Paul, Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ". Paul writes that James, Cephas and John gave him and Barnabas "the right hands of fellowship". But at Antioch, when Peter withdrew from eating with the Gentiles, "Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation".

Some days later Barnabas wanted to take John Mark on another journey, but Paul would not take one who had left them in Pamphylia. "The contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other": Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, and Paul chose Silas. Acts says no more of Barnabas. Paul names him again in 1 Corinthians, asking whether only he and Barnabas had no right "to forbear working", and in Colossians. Scripture does not record his death.

mark-act-12-12.short: "John, whose surname was Mark", from a Jerusalem house where many gathered to pray; he left Paul and Barnabas at Perga, and later sailed with Barnabas to Cyprus.

paragraphs.text: When an angel brought Peter out of prison, Peter came to "the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying". That is the first time Scripture names him. It names his mother but never his father.

Barnabas and Saul, coming back from Jerusalem, took John with them, and when the two set out from Antioch for Cyprus, "they had also John to their minister". After Paphos the company came to Perga in Pamphylia, and "John departing from them returned to Jerusalem". Acts does not say why.

Some days later Barnabas wanted to take him on another journey, but Paul "thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work". The contention was so sharp that the two went separate ways: "Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus". Acts says no more of him.

Paul's letters name a Marcus whom Colossians calls "sister's son to Barnabas"; the Revised Version renders the Greek word as cousin. Acts does not call John Mark a relative of Barnabas, but his page takes this Marcus to be the same man. Paul tells the Colossians to receive him if he comes, and counts him among the few "of the circumcision" who were his "fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God" and "a comfort" to him. In Philemon he is one of Paul's "fellowlabourers", and in 2 Timothy Paul writes, "Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry."

Peter's first letter sends greetings from "Marcus my son"; Scripture does not say whether this is the same Mark. It does not say how Mark came to believe or how he died. The Gospel of Mark does not name its writer; who wrote it is taken up on Mark's page.
